newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy seeks to smooth ruffles over its EMU hopes.
newsitem.headline: Italy seeks to smooth ruffles over its EMU hopes.

text.p: Italy denied on Monday that it had tried to talk Spain into seeking a softening of the tough criteria for entry to monetary union and dismissed reports that its EU partners had been trying to stop it joining a single currency.
"No-one wants Italy out of the euro," Treasury and Budget Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said in Washington where he is attending the IMF and World Bank annual meetings.

Italy unveiled a harder-than-expected 1997 budget last week to try to meet the economic goals in the Maastricht Treaty that are pre-requesites for joining a single currency, to be called the euro, which is set for launch in 1999.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose package has sparked criticism from opposition and business leaders, denied he recently tried to convince his Spanish counterpart Jose Maria Aznar to try to persade EU partners to modify some criteria.

A government statement said Prodi had telephoned Aznar on Monday afternoon after the Financial Times quoted the Spanish leader as saying Italy had wanted the two countries to "walk together holding hands towards Maastricht."
"The proposals for collaboration between Italy and Spain referred to several sectors...and certainly did not presume joint actions to soften the Maastricht criteria," it said.
Aznar told the Financial Times: "I am not interested in holding hands. I told him we'd be there right at the start."

Italy is determined to make the first wave of countries, even though Sunday newspapers quoted Prodi as saying it could still overshoot a key three percent ratio of deficit to gross domestic product in 1997, despite the stringent budget.
Finance Minister Vincenzo Visco said earlier some European states had speeded up their efforts to try to keep Italy out.

Visco told a news conference that the government had changed its approach budget earlier this month. He said that was because of "an acceleration towards convergence in some countries linked not only to the conviction but also to the hope and desire that our country would be excluded." He would not name the countries.
Italy, a founder member of the original European Economic Community (EEC), has historically been acutely sensitive to any suggestion that it is not the equal of its European partners.
But Ciampi dismissed Visco's comments as well as news reports that French President Jacques Chirac might be against Italy's participation in the euro on stability grounds.
"Chirac said exactly the opposite," Ciampi told reporters.

Italy's budget, which now goes to parliament, aims to cut 62.5 trillion lire ($41 billion) from next year's deficit, almost double the centre-left government's initial target. It also includes a special one-off "Euro-tax" to raise 13 trillion lire.
